title: The Two Ewes
intro: Two ewes graze in one field. One likes what people say about the price she would fetch, while her thin sister bears the comparison in silence. The arrival of a man prepared to pay that price changes what it means to be a valuable sheep. The reciter gives the lean sister’s closing lesson a second hearing.

translation: Someone once owned two ewes.
They grazed together in the field.
1.sharh: The opening puts the two animals on exactly the same patch of ground. The Arabic verbs both carry a special ending for a pair.

translation: One was fat. The other
showed every bone beneath her skin.
2.sharh: The fat ewe needs only one adjective. The lean one has to endure a longer, closer look, the very indignity on which her sister thrives.

translation: The first boasted of her plumpness
and the price people said she would fetch.
3.sharh: She enjoys hearing strangers put a price on her. That pleasure depends on never following the bargain as far as the buyer.

translation: She claimed to be a creature of consequence
who could arrest a passing gaze.
4.sharh: Her claims move from the market to the admiring gaze. We can already imagine another reason why a passer-by might stop and look at a well-fed sheep.

translation: Her sister bore the humiliation patiently,
swallowing the bitterness of her airs.
5.sharh: A change from dh to d turns the humiliation inflicted on the thin sister into the self-important airs of the fat one. The two similar sounds carry the two sides of a single encounter.

translation: Until one day the butcher came
and singled out the ewe, turning her about to inspect her.
6.sharh: The butcher singles out the ewe and handles her. She has succeeded in attracting attention of the most exacting kind.

translation: “I’ll buy her,” he told the owner,
and paid him a whole purseful for her.
7.sharh: The owner receives the money. The ewe’s high price has become real, and the whole benefit of it belongs to someone else.

translation: At once she hurried to her sister,
no longer sure how good her fortune was.
8.sharh: The confident boast has dwindled to a doubt. For the first time the ewe needs a judgement on her prospects from the sister whose opinion she discounted.

translation: “Sister dear, tell me,
do you know the man who carries the knife?”
9.sharh: The reader knows the buyer’s trade already. The fat ewe can name the knife but cannot yet bring herself to say what it is for.

translation: “Leave me to my leanness and to time.
Talk to the butcher, you ewe of such a price.
10.sharh: The lean ewe hands back the very phrase her sister prized. The butcher can now explain the market value of fatness more accurately than anyone else in the field.

translation: Each lot has its sweetness and its bitter taste.
A ewe’s whole schooling lies in patience.”
11.sharh: The earlier bitterness of humiliation comes back as one taste among several. The ewe who endured it can give the lesson, and the performance repeats her words.

1.2.3.head: الغَيط
1.2.3.meaning: A cultivated field, a word familiar from rural Egypt.

2.2.3.head: الهُزال
2.2.3.meaning: Leanness or emaciation that makes the bones show.

2.2.4.head: بادِيَة
2.2.4.meaning: Plainly visible. The word describes the bones showing through.

3.1.3.head: باهى
3.1.3.meaning: Boasted, made an ostentatious comparison in one’s own favour.

3.2.3-4.head: ذات ثَمَن
3.2.3-4.meaning: “One who fetches a price”. The reciter gives the noun without its article. Both diwans have “the price” here, the same form the lean sister uses in couplet 10.

4.1.4.head: مِقدار
4.1.4.meaning: Consequence or social standing, as the ewe understands it.

4.2.2.head: اِستَوقَفَ
4.2.2.meaning: Arrested someone’s attention, made someone stop and look.

4.2.3.head: الأَبصار
4.2.3.meaning: The onlookers’ eyes, including those of someone sizing her up for purchase.

5.1.4.head: الإِذلال
5.1.4.meaning: Humiliation endured by the thin sister. The performance follows the Beirut printing. Hindawi reverses the two near-identical nouns.

5.2.3.head: الإِدلال
5.2.3.meaning: Presumptuous, self-important behaviour, the airs put on by the fat sister.

6.2.1.head: قَلَّبَ
6.2.1.meaning: Turned an animal about to inspect its condition before buying.

6.2.3-4.head: دونَ القَوم
6.2.3-4.meaning: “Apart from the company”, singled out for the buyer’s inspection.

7.2.2-3.head: الكيس النَّفيس
7.2.2-3.meaning: “The precious purse”, the substantial sum contained in it.

8.1.2-3.meaning: At once, without pausing to consider.

8.2.4.head: صَلاح
8.2.4.meaning: The favourable turn of her fortunes, the sense of “goodness” in this expression.

8.2.5.head: بَخت
8.2.5.meaning: Fortune or luck, a word borrowed from Persian.

9.1.3.head: أُختاه
9.1.3.meaning: Dear sister, an extended form of address that catches the note of appeal.

9.2.3-4.head: حامِل السِّكّين
9.2.3-4.meaning: “The man carrying the knife”. The ewe can name his tool before she can bring herself to name his trade.

10.1.4.head: الزَّمَن
10.1.4.meaning: Time and whatever it may bring, the lean ewe’s chosen companion.

10.2.4-5.head: ذات الثَّمَن
10.2.4-5.meaning: “You ewe of such a price”. The lean sister gives the boast back to its owner when the buyer has a knife in hand.

11.1.3.head: حُلو
11.1.3.meaning: Sweetness, the part of one’s lot one finds pleasing.

11.2.2.head: أَدَب
11.2.2.meaning: The training of character or good conduct exemplified by the lean ewe’s patience.
